GPT-5.4 Came for Claude Code. The Real Story Is Bigger Than Both

Han HELOIR YAN, Ph.D. ☕️

Models are commoditizing. The war moved to the runtime layer. Here’s what that means for your workflow

Free link =>If this helped, I’d really appreciate your full 50 claps. It supports my work and helps others find it.

GPT-5.4 was released yesterday. OpenAI shipped native computer use, a 1M-token context window, and a new Tool Search feature that cuts token costs in half, and aimed the whole package directly at Claude Code.

The benchmarks look strong. The pricing is competitive. If you follow the headlines, you’d think this is about model quality.

It’s not.

Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.3-Codex, and now GPT-5.4 — four frontier models in a single month. GPT-5.x has had four releases in four months. The cadence itself is the signal. Pretraining scaling hit a wall, models are commoditizing, and the war moved one layer up: who captures your workflow.

This article is the day-after field notes from a builder who uses both models.

TL;DR

  • GPT-5.4 unifies coding, reasoning, and computer use in one model — but the coding benchmark gain is only +2.1 points. The real moves are computer use (+27.7 pts on OSWorld) and token efficiency (Tool Search saves 47%).
  • The rapid release cadence is not a sign of breakthroughs. It’s a sign that pretraining scaling plateaued and every lab pivoted to shipping product-layer moves faster.
  • Models are commoditizing. The same MCP protocol and SKILL.md format now work across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Cursor. The fight moved above the model layer.
  • Claude Code went from $0 to $2.5B revenue in nine months and holds 54% of enterprise coding market share. GPT-5.4 is a direct counterattack against this.
  • OpenAI bets on broad unification at the model layer (one model does everything). Anthropic bets on deep specialization at the runtime layer (terminal-native agents, sub-agents, 9,000+ plugins). Different layers, different problems.
  • The honest builder move: route by task complexity, not brand loyalty. Use GPT-5.4 the model for speed. Use Claude Code the runtime for depth. Wait for independent benchmarks before making infrastructure decisions.

What GPT-5.4 Actually Ships

OpenAI released GPT-5.4 on March 5, 2026, calling it “our most capable and efficient frontier model for professional work.” Three model variants are available: standard GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 Thinking (reasoning-focused, available in ChatGPT), and GPT-5.4 Pro (maximum performance via API, at $30/$180 per million tokens).

The headline features look like a direct response to Anthropic’s coding products.

Native computer use is the most striking addition. GPT-5.4 scores 75.0% on OSWorld-Verified — a +27.7 point jump from GPT-5.2’s 47.3%, and it surpasses the human baseline of 72.4%. The model can operate computers through both Playwright code and direct mouse/keyboard commands from screenshots. No previous general-purpose OpenAI model shipped with this capability built in.

Tool Search is a structural efficiency fix for the API. Instead of loading all tool definitions upfront (burning thousands of tokens), GPT-5.4 receives a lightweight tool list and retrieves full definitions on demand. Across 250 tasks from Scale’s MCP Atlas benchmark with 36 MCP servers enabled, this reduced total token usage by 47% while maintaining the same accuracy. If you run large tool ecosystems, that’s a real cost cut.

1M token context is now experimentally available in Codex, though requests exceeding 272,000 tokens are billed at double rates.

Here’s what the benchmarks actually say — and how GPT-5.4 stacks up against Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro:

The pattern is clear — and it’s not “one model wins everything.” GPT-5.4 leads on computer use, terminal execution, and professional tasks. Opus 4.6 leads on coding and visual reasoning. Gemini 3.1 Pro leads on scientific and abstract reasoning. No single model dominates across the board.

The coding story is the most telling. On SWE-Bench Verified — the benchmark most relevant to the complex coding tasks developers use Claude Code for — Opus 4.6 the model sits at 80.8%. GPT-5.4 the model doesn’t even publish a Verified score, and its Pro variant (SWE-Bench Pro at 57.7%) lags well behind Opus. That model-level gap matters — but remember, Claude Code’s competitive position also lives in its runtime layer (sub-agents, MCP, hooks), not just the model underneath.

Pricing is competitive on the standard tier: $2.50 input / $15 output per million tokens vs Claude Opus 4.6 at $5/$25. The Pro variant is a different story — at $30/$180, it’s more than 7x the standard price and significantly more expensive than Opus.

What’s not verified yet: all these benchmarks are OpenAI-reported. As of March 6, 2026, no independent third-party results exist on Arena.ai or Artificial Analysis. Treat the numbers as directional until independent validation lands.

Why Releases Come This Fast

GPT-5.1 in November. GPT-5.2 in December. GPT-5.3-Codex in February. GPT-5.4 in March. Four point-releases in four months. Meanwhile, Anthropic shipped Claude 4.5 and 4.6. Google shipped Gemini 3 and 3.1. In February alone, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, and GPT-5.3-Codex all shipped. Now GPT-5.4 landed in early March. Four frontier models in roughly one month.

This cadence is not normal. And it’s not because the labs discovered four breakthroughs in a row.

The real cause is that pretraining scaling hit diminishing returns. OpenAI’s internal next-gen model (Orion) showed far smaller gains than the jump from GPT-3 to GPT-4. Google’s Gemini team reportedly saw “disappointing results” from their next training run. Research from UC Berkeley (Snell et al.) confirmed what the labs were seeing internally: on easy and medium tasks, spending more compute at inference often beats spending it on pretraining.

Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI’s former chief scientist, put it bluntly: “The 2010s were the age of scaling. Now we’re back in the age of wonder and discovery.”

So the labs pivoted. Not to one new thing — to three:

  1. Post-training RL — reinforcement learning after pretraining to sharpen specific capabilities (reasoning, coding, tool use)
  2. Test-time compute — spending more compute at inference to “think longer” instead of training larger models
  3. Agent capabilities — computer use, tool search, multi-step workflows — product-layer features that don’t require a new base model

Here’s the counterintuitive truth: every GPT-5.4 headline feature is an inference-time innovation. Tool Search saves tokens at inference. Computer use runs screenshot→action loops at inference. Thinking mode extends reasoning at inference. The 1M context window processes more data at inference. None of these required a fundamentally larger or smarter base model — they required a better product wrapping.

This explains the rapid cadence. When your primary innovation loop moves from “train a bigger model” (18-month cycle) to “ship a better product layer” (weeks-to-months cycle), you can release much more frequently. Every release is a product-layer move, not a training breakthrough.

Financial pressure amplifies the velocity. OpenAI raised $110B at an $840B valuation in February 2026 while projecting $14B in losses for the year. Anthropic’s revenue hit $14B annualized by the same month, growing 10x year-over-year for three consecutive years. The race for market share doesn’t wait for the next pretraining run.

OpenAI engineers leave for Anthropic at an 8:1 ratio. OpenAI’s retention rate is 67% versus Anthropic’s 80%. When your talent is leaving and your investors need proof of momentum, you ship faster — regardless of whether you have a training breakthrough to ship.

The honest takeaway: stop treating each release as a capability step-change. Treat it as a product iteration. The models are not getting dramatically smarter per training dollar. They’re getting dramatically more efficient at using what they already know.

The Real War Is One Layer Up

If models are commoditizing and benchmarks are converging, where did the competition go?

Follow the money. Claude Code went from zero revenue to $2.5B annualized in approximately nine months. Claude holds 54% of the enterprise coding market — more than double OpenAI’s 21%. Anthropic overtook OpenAI in enterprise LLM market share overall: 32% versus 25%, down from OpenAI’s 50% just two years ago.

GPT-5.4 targeting Claude Code is not a model-quality play. It’s a market-share recovery play.

The MCP convergence is the clearest proof. Anthropic created the Model Context Protocol in November 2024. By March 2025, OpenAI adopted it across the Agents SDK, Responses API, and ChatGPT desktop. By December 2025, both companies co-founded the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation to govern MCP as a shared standard. Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and dozens of enterprise companies joined as members.

When your competitor adopts your protocol — and then co-founds a foundation with you to maintain it — the competition is no longer at the protocol layer. It moved above it.

Skills tell the same story. In December 2025, Anthropic released the Agent Skills specification as an open standard. OpenAI adopted the same SKILL.md format for Codex CLI. The same skill now runs on Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and Windsurf. Over 350,000 skills are indexed on SkillsMP alone. Claude Code's plugin ecosystem has grown to 9,000+ packages.

The model underneath is becoming interchangeable plumbing. The differentiation is now:

  • Who has the richest ecosystem — Claude Code: 9,000+ plugins, 5.2M VS Code installs (vs Codex 4.9M)
  • Who has the best agent runtime — sub-agents, hooks, Agent Teams, permission models
  • Who captures the developer workflow — once your team builds around one tool’s MCP servers, hooks, and CLAUDE.md conventions, switching costs are real

This is not a theoretical observation. It’s already visible in adoption. Despite being published months after Codex CLI, Claude Code leads in VS Code installs (5.2M vs 4.9M) and ratings (4.0 vs 3.4 on a 5-point scale). The ecosystem moat is forming now.

The real insight: the next time a new model drops and the benchmarks look impressive, ask yourself whether it changes the agent runtime, the ecosystem, or the workflow capture. If it only changes the model scores, the competitive impact is smaller than the press release suggests.

Two Bets, Two Architectures

If the model layer is commoditizing and the protocol layer is shared, why do Claude Code and Codex CLI feel so different to use? Because they’re built on fundamentally different architectural philosophies.

OpenAI’s bet with GPT-5.4: consolidate everything into one model. Coding from GPT-5.3-Codex. Reasoning from the o-series. Computer use from Operator. Tool Search for efficiency. One unified model, cloud-first, token-efficient. The pitch to developers: you don’t need to think about which model to use — GPT-5.4 handles all of it. The business logic: 900M weekly users, a potential IPO in Q4 2026, and a platform play that scales through breadth.

Anthropic’s bet with Claude Code: go deep on the agent layer. The model (Opus 4.6) is excellent, but it’s not the product. The product is the terminal-native runtime: sub-agents that delegate tasks with their own prompts and permissions, Agent Teams for parallel coordination across sessions, MCP servers that pull context from Jira, Google Docs, and Slack mid-session, and a plugin ecosystem with 9,000+ packages. The business logic: 85% revenue from enterprise, 54% of coding market, positive cash flow by 2027.

These are not competing on the same axis. One optimizes for breadth — do everything adequately in one model. The other optimizes for depth — do complex software engineering exceptionally well through a rich agent layer.

The difference shows up in daily use. Codex CLI is open-source (Rust), fast, and has a clean three-tier permission model: Suggest, Auto-Edit, Full Auto. You point it at a task and it executes quickly. Claude Code requires more upfront investment — CLAUDE.md files, hook configuration, sub-agent setup — but once configured, it handles multi-file features that touch frontend, backend, database, and docs in a single workflow.

The engineering cultures they optimize for are different too. Codex CLI fits teams that want speed, low friction, and a “fast intern” for quick iterations. Claude Code fits teams that need a “senior developer” for architectural reasoning, complex refactoring, and deep codebase understanding.

The honest framing: this is not a “who’s better” question. It’s a “what problem are you solving” question.

One signal to watch: convergence. Codex CLI recently added MCP support and a skills system. Claude Code recently added /fast mode and speed optimizations. Both are drifting toward each other's strengths. The question for 2026 is whether the architectural split deepens — or whether both tools end up doing the same thing, differentiated only by ecosystem lock-in.

There’s a blind spot in both philosophies worth naming. Both OpenAI and Anthropic frame the world as “you need our frontier model.” But the majority of real-world applications — classification, summarization, extraction, customer-facing chat, structured data pipelines — don’t need a frontier model at all. Smaller, specialized, open-weight models often deliver better latency, lower cost, tighter deployment control, and equivalent quality for scoped tasks. The coding agent battle between GPT-5.4 and Claude Code is real, but it’s one slice of a much larger landscape where the right answer is frequently a smaller model fine-tuned for the job, not the biggest model available.

Where Each One Actually Wins (And Why “Best Model” Is the Wrong Question)

Here’s the uncomfortable truth that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic’s marketing will tell you: no single model wins everything. Not GPT-5.4. Not Opus 4.6. Not Gemini 3.1 Pro. The benchmarks make this clear — each model tops different categories, and the gaps are often within margin of error.

But there’s a second layer the benchmarks don’t capture at all: the runtime — the agent layer that sits on top of the model. And this is where the conversation gets confused. People say “Claude Code wins at multi-file refactoring.” That’s partly Opus 4.6 the model, but mostly Claude Code the runtime — sub-agents, hooks, MCP context. Separating these two layers matters, because the model is becoming interchangeable. The runtime is not.

Image by Author — Honest scorecard: model-level wins vs runtime-level wins, separated for clarity

Model-level wins — GPT-5.4:

  • Token efficiency. ~4x fewer tokens on identical tasks. At $2.50/$15 per million tokens vs Opus 4.6’s $5/$25, the cost gap is real for high-volume teams.
  • Computer use. 75% on OSWorld — a model capability baked into GPT-5.4 itself, not a runtime feature.
  • Speed on simple tasks. 3–5x faster inference on quick fixes, scripts, prototypes. This is model-level throughput.

Model-level wins — Opus 4.6:

  • Complex coding. 80.8% on SWE-bench Verified. The model itself reasons better across multi-file codebases.
  • Visual reasoning. 85.1% on MMMU Pro — highest among all three frontier models.
  • Deep architectural reasoning. On tasks where thoroughness matters more than speed, Opus 4.6’s extended thinking produces more reliable outputs.

Model-level wins — Gemini 3.1 Pro:

  • Scientific reasoning. 94.3% on GPQA Diamond — the highest score across all three.
  • Abstract reasoning. 77.1% on ARC-AGI-2.
  • Context window. 1M tokens native, no double-billing on the first 272K.

Runtime-level wins — Codex CLI:

  • Open-source. Rust codebase, auditable, extensible.
  • GitHub-native. PR auto-review, CI/CD integration, built for the GitHub workflow.
  • Low friction. Three-tier permission model (Suggest, Auto-Edit, Full Auto). Minimal configuration.

Runtime-level wins — Claude Code:

  • Agent orchestration. Five sub-agent types, Agent Teams for parallel sessions, hooks for lifecycle control. No other coding runtime matches this depth.
  • MCP ecosystem. 9,000+ plugins, 350,000+ indexed skills. Jira, Slack, Google Docs, Confluence — all available as live context mid-session.
  • Enterprise workflow capture. CLAUDE.md conventions, per-tool permissions, deep configuration. Once set up, the switching costs are real.

The tie zones — and these are growing: general coding on single files, standard reasoning tasks, code review on small PRs. Here, the models are close enough that personal preference and ecosystem fit matter more than benchmarks.

Zoom out further, and the scorecard itself reveals the structural shift: models are commoditizing in real time.

Eighteen months ago, you picked a model and built around it. Today, the smart teams I talk to are doing something different — they’re routing tasks to different models based on what each one does best. Quick script? GPT-5.4. Complex refactor? Opus 4.6 through Claude Code’s runtime. Research synthesis? Gemini 3.1 Pro with its 1M context window. Each model as a specialized engine, not a universal solution.

But here’s what the frontier model scorecard doesn’t show: most production applications don’t need a frontier model at all. The coding agent use case — the one this article focuses on — genuinely benefits from the largest, most capable models. Multi-file reasoning, architectural planning, and complex refactoring push the limits of what models can do. But step outside the coding agent bubble, and the landscape changes completely.

Classification, summarization, extraction, structured data pipelines, customer-facing chat, content moderation, translation — these tasks run in production at scale, and they run best on smaller, specialized models. Open-weight models. Fine-tuned models. Models optimized for latency, cost, and deployment flexibility rather than benchmark scores. A well-tuned 7B model serving a specific extraction task at 10ms latency and $0.10/M tokens will outperform a frontier model at $25/M tokens for that use case — not on benchmarks, but on the metrics that matter in production: cost per query, latency at p99, and deployment control.

The commoditization thesis extends further than the big three. It’s not just “GPT-5.4 vs Opus 4.6 vs Gemini 3.1 Pro.” It’s “frontier models for frontier tasks, specialized models for everything else.” The teams building the most robust production systems aren’t choosing between OpenAI and Anthropic — they’re building model-agnostic architectures where a frontier model handles the hard reasoning and a smaller model handles the 80% of tasks that don’t need it.

This is the logical endpoint of the commoditization trend from Section 3. If every frontier model converges on similar capabilities — and they are converging — then the “best model” question stops being useful. The answer is always “for what?” And for most production workloads, the answer isn’t the biggest model in the room.

The teams getting the most value right now aren’t loyal to one model or one runtime. They’re building model-agnostic workflows where the agent runtime routes to whatever model handles that specific task best. MCP and SKILL.md make this possible at the protocol level. The runtime layer makes it practical.

This is the real shift. Not “GPT-5.4 killed Claude Code” or “Claude Code is still king.” The shift is: the era of one model to rule them all is ending. The era of intelligent task routing is beginning. And the runtimes that win will be the ones that make that routing seamless — not the ones that insist their model is the only one you need.

What I’d Actually Change in My Workflow

So after all the benchmarks, architecture diagrams, and commoditization theory — what would I actually do differently starting Monday?

Short answer: I’d stop using one tool for everything.

Here’s the honest version of my current setup and where I’d shift it — separating what’s a model decision from what’s a runtime decision.

What stays with Claude Code (runtime wins):

  • Multi-file features. Anything that touches frontend + backend + tests + docs in one go. This is Claude Code’s sub-agent architecture earning its keep — not just the Opus 4.6 model, but the runtime coordinating changes across 12 files in a single session with the right CLAUDE.md configuration. Codex CLI’s runtime can’t orchestrate that yet.
  • MCP-heavy sessions. When I need Jira context, Slack threads, and Google Docs all feeding into a coding session, Claude Code’s 9,000+ plugin ecosystem isn’t a nice-to-have — it’s load-bearing infrastructure. This is a runtime advantage, not a model advantage.
  • Architecture decisions. Migration planning, dependency analysis, “should we split this service” conversations. Here it’s both — the Opus 4.6 model’s thoroughness at $25/M output tokens, plus Claude Code’s deep context management.

What I’d move to GPT-5.4 + Codex CLI (model wins + runtime fit):

  • Quick scripts and one-off fixes. GPT-5.4 the model is 3–5x faster. For “write me a bash script to clean up these log files” or “fix this off-by-one error,” the model’s speed advantage is real and Codex CLI’s low-friction runtime matches.
  • PR reviews on small-to-medium PRs. Lower token cost (model advantage) plus Codex CLI’s GitHub-native integration (runtime advantage) make this the better combination for the volume game.
  • Computer automation tasks. GUI testing, form filling, desktop app scripting — GPT-5.4 the model scores 75% on OSWorld. This is a genuine model-level capability that Claude Code’s terminal-native runtime doesn’t surface.

What doesn’t need a frontier model at all:

  • Production APIs that classify, extract, or summarize. If you’re running a data pipeline that extracts structured fields from documents, a fine-tuned smaller model will be faster, cheaper, and easier to deploy than any frontier model. Don’t use a $15/M token model for a $0.10/M token task.
  • Customer-facing chat with scoped domains. A well-tuned open-weight model with a focused knowledge base often delivers better latency and consistency than a frontier model that knows everything but takes 3 seconds to respond.
  • Content moderation, translation, structured output generation. These are solved problems at the smaller model tier. Frontier models add cost without adding quality.

This is the part the GPT-5.4 vs Claude Code framing misses entirely. Yes, coding agents need frontier reasoning. But most of the software you’re building on top of these agents will serve users through smaller, specialized models. The architecture should reflect that — frontier models for development, right-sized models for production.

What I’d watch before committing:

  • Independent benchmarks. Every number in this article comes from the vendors themselves or early third-party reports. I want to see Aider, BigCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench results on GPT-5.4 before I trust the benchmarks fully.
  • Token cost at scale. 4x efficiency sounds great — but does it hold on complex tasks, or only on simple ones? The devil is in the distribution.
  • MCP maturity on Codex CLI. It’s new. Claude Code’s MCP has been battle-tested for months. Give it a quarter.

The uncomfortable truth: the era of single-tool loyalty is over. Sticking with one model and one runtime for everything because “it’s the best” is leaving performance on the table. The teams I see shipping fastest in early 2026 are already running hybrid setups — picking the right model for the task (GPT-5.4 for speed, Opus 4.6 for depth, Gemini 3.1 Pro for research) and the right runtime for the workflow (Codex CLI for GitHub-native speed, Claude Code for orchestrated depth).

The one thing I wouldn’t do: migrate an existing Claude Code workflow to GPT-5.4 based on a launch-day blog post. The benchmarks need independent verification. The MCP support needs production testing. The token efficiency claims need real-world validation on complex tasks, not cherry-picked demos.

Build the hybrid. Route by task type. Wait for the independent data before going all-in on anything. That’s the honest advice.
